title: Variation of Length with Velocity (Length Contraction)
short_intro: Length contraction, also known as Lorentz-FitzGerald contraction, is the phenomenon where the measured length of an object is shorter when it is moving relative to the observer than when it is at rest. It is a fundamental consequence of the constancy of the speed of light in all inertial frames of reference as established by Einstein's special theory of relativity.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Conceptual understanding of proper length versus contracted length, formula identification, identification of velocity dependence, and direct numerical substitution using the gamma factor.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of length contraction using Lorentz transformations, simultaneous measurement definition, spatial and temporal coordinate relations, and application to moving high-energy particles (muons).

prerequisites: Postulates of Special Theory of Relativity

concept_notes.heading: Proper Length vs. Relativistic Length
bullets: Proper length (L<sub>0</sub>) is the length of an object measured in the frame of reference in which the object is at rest.
Relativistic or contracted length (L) is the length measured by an observer moving at a constant relative velocity v with respect to the object.
Length contraction occurs strictly along the direction of relative motion; dimensions perpendicular to the motion remain unaffected.

concept_notes.heading: Physical Interpretation of Lorentz Factor
bullets: The contraction is governed by the Lorentz factor gamma where γ = (1 - v<sup>2</sup>/c<sup>2</sup>)<sup>-1/2</sup>.
As the relative velocity v approaches the speed of light c, the contracted length approaches zero.
Length contraction is a reciprocal phenomenon; each observer in uniform relative motion perceives the other's measuring rods as contracted.

concept_notes.heading: Simultaneity and Measurement
bullets: Measuring the length of a moving object requires determining the positions of both ends simultaneously in the observer's frame.
Events that are simultaneous in the object's rest frame are generally not simultaneous in the moving observer's frame.
This failure of simultaneity is the physical origin of why length contraction occurs.

concept_notes.heading: Anisotropy of Length Contraction
bullets: If a rod makes an angle with the direction of motion, only its component parallel to the velocity vector undergoes contraction.
The transverse component of length remains invariant, i.e., y = y<sub>0</sub> and z = z<sub>0</sub>.
Consequently, the orientation and shape of moving objects appear distorted to a stationary observer.

derivations.title: Derivation of Length Contraction using Lorentz Transformations
derivations.conditions: Rod is at rest in frame S' moving with velocity v along the x-axis relative to frame S.
steps: Let the proper length of the rod in S' be L<sub>0</sub> = x'_2 - x'_1, where x'_1 and x'_2 are the coordinates of the ends of the rod in S'.
Using the Lorentz coordinate transformation, relate the coordinates in S to S': x' = γ(x - vt).
An observer in frame S measures the positions of the two ends of the rod simultaneously at a single instant of time t (so t_1 = t_2 = t).
Therefore, the length measured in S is L = x_2 - x_1.
Substitute the transformation equations: x'_1 = γ(x_1 - vt) and x'_2 = γ(x_2 - vt).
Subtract the two equations to get L<sub>0</sub> = x'_2 - x'_1 = γ(x_2 - x_1) = γL.
Rearrange to express the contracted length in terms of proper length: L = L_0 / γ.

derivations.title: Transverse Length Invariance
derivations.conditions: Rod or object oriented perpendicular to the direction of motion.
steps: Consider an object of length y<sub>0</sub> placed along the y-axis in frame S', moving along the x-axis relative to S.
The Lorentz transformation for the y-coordinate is simply y = y'.
Since there is no relative motion along the y-axis or z-axis, measuring instruments oriented transversely experience no spatial compression.
Therefore, y<sub>0</sub> measured in S' equals y measured in S.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Length vs. Velocity Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of L/L_0 on the y-axis versus v/c on the x-axis ranging from 0 to 1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows a horizontal line at 1 for low speeds, curving downward smoothly as v/c increases, and plunging sharply to zero as v approaches c.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT/PGT to identify limiting behaviors at non-relativistic and ultra-relativistic speeds.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Muon Decay Atmospheric Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of cosmic ray muons generated in upper atmosphere reaching the Earth's surface.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: From the Earth's frame, the atmospheric height is contracted, allowing short-lived muons to reach the ground within their lifetime.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Standard PGT application question confirming physical reality of length contraction.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rod Orientation Distortion
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular coordinate grid showing a tilted square rod in rest frame transformed into a sheared rectangle in moving frame.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that longitudinal contraction combined with transverse invariance alters the perceived geometric angles of moving objects.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced PGT conceptual multiple-choice questions on spatial anisotropy.

solved_numericals.question: A rod has a proper length of 2 m. At what speed must it move so that its length appears to be 1 m to a stationary observer?
solution_steps: Identify given values: Proper length L_0 = 2 m, Contracted length L = 1 m.
Use the length contraction formula: L = L_0 * sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).

solved_numericals.question: A spaceship of rest length 100 m passes an observer at a speed of 0.6c. What is the length of the spaceship as measured by the observer, and what is the time taken by the spaceship to pass a stationary point for that observer?
solution_steps: Identify proper length L_0 = 100 m and velocity v = 0.6c.
Calculate the contracted length: L = L_0 * sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 100 * sqrt(1 - (0.6)^2) = 100 * sqrt(1 - 0.36) = 100 * sqrt(0.64) = 100 * 0.8 = 80 m.
Calculate the time taken to pass a stationary point: t = L / v.
Substitute L = 80 m and v = 0.6 * 3 * 10^8 m/s = 1.8 * 10^8 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: A square plate of side 2 m is moving with a velocity of 0.8c along one of its edges parallel to the x-axis. Find the area of the plate as measured by a stationary observer.
solution_steps: Identify proper dimensions: L_x0 = 2 m, L_y0 = 2 m. Proper area A_0 = L_x0 * L_y0 = 4 m^2.
Motion is along the x-axis, so only the dimension parallel to x contracts: L_x = L_x0 * sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
Calculate contraction factor: sqrt(1 - (0.8)^2) = sqrt(1 - 0.64) = sqrt(0.36) = 0.6.
Contracted length along x: L_x = 2 * 0.6 = 1.2 m.
Transverse length remains unchanged: L_y = L_y0 = 2 m.
Calculate measured area: A = L_x * L_y = 1.2 * 2 = 2.4 m^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes uniform relative motion between two inertial frames of reference in empty space.
Valid only for speeds comparable to the speed of light (v approaching c); breaks down in classical mechanics limits where v << c.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Length contraction is an optical illusion caused by the time light takes to travel from the object to the eye.
common_misconceptions.correct: Length contraction is a real physical kinematic effect of spacetime geometry, independent of visual perception.
common_misconceptions.why: It arises directly from the Lorentz transformation of spatial coordinates under simultaneous measurement protocols.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An object physically shrinks or experiences internal mechanical stress when it moves.
common_misconceptions.correct: No internal stress is created simply by moving at constant velocity in an inertial frame.
common_misconceptions.why: Motion is relative; in the object's own rest frame, its dimensions are completely normal.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Contraction occurs in all directions around a moving object.
common_misconceptions.correct: Contraction is strictly unidirectional, occurring exclusively along the axis of relative motion.
common_misconceptions.why: Components perpendicular to the velocity vector remain identical in all inertial frames.

quick_revision: Length contraction states that moving objects appear shortened along the direction of motion: L = L_0 / \gamma.
